specPoints.text: describe uses of radioactivity in industry and medicine

primer.text: Choose the radiation to fit the job: alpha’s strong ionisation runs smoke detectors, beta’s partial absorption gauges foil thickness, gamma’s deep reach treats tumours and sterilises equipment. Industry and medicine simply exploit the property table from the last topic.

lessons.title: Smoke detectors and thickness gauges
lessons.opening: Smoke detectors rely on alpha ionising the air to hold a small current; smoke blocks the alpha and the alarm fires. Thickness gauges rely on beta partly penetrating foil: thicker foil, fewer counts — so the detector’s reading steers the rollers.
keyPoints: Smoke detectors use alpha radiation to ionise air and sustain a current.
Smoke absorbs the alpha, the current stops, and the alarm triggers.
Beta radiation monitors foil thickness because foil partially absorbs it.
Thicker material absorbs more beta, so the count rate falls; thinner raises it.
Alpha would be fully absorbed at any foil thickness; gamma would pass almost unaffected.

low.restatement: Detector: alpha current always on until smoke eats it. Gauge: beta always partly through until thicker foil eats more.
low.analogy: Alpha in a detector is a tripwire that any smoke cuts; beta in a gauge is a flowmeter whose reading tracks the foil’s thickness.
low.examPointer: The classic "why alpha, not beta or gamma" answer: smoke absorbs alpha easily; beta/gamma would pass straight through and never trigger.

medium.restatement: The choice is a matching exercise between penetration and signal sensitivity: alpha gives a huge, easily-cancelled ion current in still air; beta’s partial absorption turns thickness into a proportional count change, giving a feedback signal with enough dynamic range to control rollers in real time.
medium.analogy: Choosing radiation is choosing a dimmer: alpha is an on/off switch (detector), beta is a smooth dial (gauge), gamma would be a light shining through the wall regardless.
medium.examPointer: For gauge questions name both directions: thicker → fewer counts, thinner → more counts.

check.stem: Which radiation does a smoke detector use?

options.explanation: Alpha ionises the air inside the detector.
Beta would pass through smoke.
Gamma would pass through smoke.
Neutrons are not used in detectors.

check.stem: What triggers the smoke alarm circuit?

options.text: the sensor no longer detecting the alpha-driven current
options.explanation: Smoke blocks the alpha, cutting the current.

options.text: a rise in the alpha current
options.explanation: The current falls, not rises, when smoke enters.
Heating is not the mechanism.
No gamma is involved.

check.stem: Why is beta suited to measuring foil thickness?

options.text: because foil only partially absorbs beta, so the count rate tracks thickness
options.explanation: Partial absorption gives a usable signal range.

options.text: because beta is stopped entirely by any foil
options.explanation: Complete absorption would give a useless on/off signal.

options.text: because beta passes through everything untouched
options.explanation: That is closer to gamma’s behaviour.

options.text: because beta ionises the foil chemically
options.explanation: No chemistry is involved.

check.stem: Foil on the gauge line gets thicker. What happens to the detector count rate?

options.text: it decreases, because more beta is absorbed
options.explanation: Absorption rises with thickness.

options.text: it increases, because thicker foil emits beta
options.explanation: The foil does not emit.
The signal’s whole point is to change.
Partial absorption keeps a nonzero count.

check.stem: Why would gamma be a poor choice for the foil gauge?

options.text: because nearly all gamma would pass through regardless of thickness
options.explanation: Gamma’s deep penetration removes the signal’s sensitivity.
Gamma is detectable.

options.text: because gamma would be fully absorbed
options.explanation: That is alpha’s problem.
Gamma is weakly ionising but that is not the issue here.

check.stem: Describe how a smoke detector uses alpha radiation.
check.modelAnswer: The alpha source ionises the air so a small current flows; smoke blocks the alpha, the current stops, and the alarm sounds.

check.stem: State one medical and one industrial use of radioactivity.
check.modelAnswer: Medical: radiotherapy for cancer (or tracers for diagnosis). Industrial: monitoring the thickness of foil (or smoke detection).

check.stem: Explain why beta, rather than alpha or gamma, monitors aluminium foil thickness.
check.modelAnswer: Foil partially absorbs beta, so count-rate changes track thickness; alpha would be absorbed completely at any thickness, and gamma would pass through almost unchanged — neither gives a usable signal.

check.stem: A gauge reading rises above its set-point while making foil. Should the rollers press harder or ease off? Explain.
check.modelAnswer: A higher count rate means fewer beta particles were absorbed, so the foil is too thin — the rollers must press harder to thicken it back to the set-point.

lessons.title: Medicine and sterilisation
lessons.opening: In medicine, gamma beams reach deep tumours from rotating angles, and tracers let PET scans locate disease. In industry, gamma sterilises sealed instruments and irradiates food to kill micro-organisms — the Radura symbol marks the treated pack.
keyPoints: Radiotherapy treats cancer with beams of gamma rays aimed at the tumour.
Gamma is chosen for radiotherapy because it penetrates the body to reach the tumour.
Beams rotate around the patient to limit harm to healthy tissue.
A tracer is a radioactive isotope tracked through the body; PET scans detect its emissions.
Gamma sterilises instruments and food because it penetrates packaging and kills micro-organisms.

low.restatement: Radiotherapy: gamma beams cross-fire the tumour. Sterilisation: gamma passes through sealed packs, killing germs inside.
low.analogy: Rotating gamma beams are like torches closing in on a target from all sides — the target gets full dose, the paths only pass once.
low.examPointer: Radiotherapy is radiation treatment — do not confuse it with chemotherapy (drugs).

medium.restatement: The same deep penetration that makes gamma useful forces the rotating-beam geometry: any single fixed beam would over-dose healthy tissue en route. Sterilisation exploits the same property through packaging — the dose integrates uniformly inside sealed wrapping, killing organisms without unsealing.
medium.analogy: Gamma sterilisation is a邮 stamp soaked through an envelope — the treatment reaches the contents without opening it.
medium.examPointer: Tracer + PET = diagnosis; gamma beam = treatment. Keep the two directions distinct.

check.stem: Which radiation treats cancer from outside the body?

options.explanation: Gamma beams penetrate deeply enough to reach tumours.
Alpha cannot penetrate skin.
Beta lacks the required depth.
Neutron therapy is not the named syllabus treatment.

check.stem: Why are the gamma beams rotated around the patient?

options.text: to spread the entry dose over healthy tissue while concentrating dose on the tumour
options.explanation: Rotation protects the paths, not the target.
Rotation redistributes dose; it does not amplify it.
Tracers are a separate diagnostic tool.
Rotation does not immobilise tissue.

options.text: a radioactive isotope whose emissions are tracked through the body
options.explanation: Tracers trace movement of substances like blood.

options.text: a beam of gamma aimed at a tumour
options.explanation: That is radiotherapy.

options.text: a device that detects radiation dose
options.explanation: That is a dosemeter/badge.
That is storage shielding.

check.stem: Why is gamma preferred for sterilising sealed instruments?

options.text: because it penetrates the packaging and irradiates all sides
options.explanation: Sealed packs can be treated without opening.

options.text: because it is the weakest ioniser so it is safest
options.explanation: Sterilisation needs the killing dose, not weakness.

options.text: because alpha could also pass through the pack
options.explanation: Alpha cannot even pass paper.
Irradiation does not make objects radioactive.

check.stem: Irradiated food carries the Radura symbol. The treatment’s purpose is to…

options.text: kill micro-organisms so the food keeps longer
options.explanation: Irradiation reduces food-borne organisms.

options.text: make the food radioactive for tracing
options.explanation: Food is not made radioactive.
No heating is involved.
Flavour is not the aim.

check.stem: Name the radiation used in radiotherapy and state why it is chosen.
check.modelAnswer: Gamma rays are used because they penetrate the body deeply enough to reach the tumour.

check.stem: Explain the role of a tracer in diagnosing cancer.
check.modelAnswer: A tracer is a radioactive isotope introduced into the body; a PET scan detects its emissions to reveal the tumour’s location.

check.stem: Explain why gamma, not beta, sterilises medical equipment inside sealed packaging.
check.modelAnswer: Gamma’s deep penetration lets it pass through the wrapping and reach every surface of the instruments; beta would be stopped by the packaging and could not sterilise the contents.

check.stem: A hospital needs to sterilise single-use syringes that are pre-sealed in plastic. Justify the choice of source and note one safety outcome for patients.
check.modelAnswer: A gamma source is chosen because it irradiates through the sealed plastic from all sides, killing micro-organisms without unsealing; patients receive sterile syringes with no microbial contamination.

glossary.definition: The treatment of cancer using beams of ionising radiation, typically gamma rays.
A radioactive isotope followed through the body to image or track a process.
Killing micro-organisms on instruments or food, here by gamma irradiation.
The international symbol marking food that has been irradiated.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why a source of alpha radiation is used in smoke detectors, and not beta or gamma radiation.
steps: Alpha is the most weakly penetrating and most strongly ionising of the three radiations.
Smoke easily absorbs the alpha, so the ion current stops and the alarm triggers.
Beta or gamma would pass straight through the smoke, so the alarm would not sound.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Alpha is used because smoke absorbs it — beta and gamma would pass through and never trigger the alarm.
